title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 4

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes and the Vital Signs. Highlight the findings that suggest increased intracranial pressure (ICP).
question.explanation:
Suggest increased ICP:

Headache worst on waking and with coughing or bending: lying flat overnight and mild CO₂ retention during sleep increase cerebral blood volume; coughing and bending raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous drainage from the head.

Vomiting on waking without nausea (often projectile): pressure on the vomiting centre in the medulla.

Bilateral papilledema: swelling of the optic discs because raised CSF pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths; a reliable sign of sustained raised ICP.

Not signs of increased ICP: staring, lip smacking, tongue biting and urinary incontinence are features of the seizure; the glucose rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of the seizure. The vital signs are not those of Cushing's triad (a late sign). Her drowsiness may be postictal or due to ICP, and the personality change, word-finding difficulty and right-hand weakness are focal deficits from the lesion itself; the nurse trends all of them.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 57-year-old female client brought in by her husband after a seizure at home.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is related to the tumor's location (a focal deficit), to increased intracranial pressure (ICP), or to the seizure. Each finding may be related to more than one cause.

rows.text: Trouble finding words
Headaches worst on waking and with coughing or bending
Bitten tongue and urinary incontinence
Weaker grip in the right hand
Bilateral papilledema
Irritable and forgetful, “not herself”
Drowsy and slow to answer in the emergency department

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Diagnostic Results and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Tumor location (focal deficits): a left frontotemporal tumor affects language (word-finding difficulty), movement of the opposite (right) side, and the frontal lobe's control of personality and memory. The nurse documents these as her baseline and watches for change.

Increased ICP: the tumor and the swelling around it take up space (Monro-Kellie doctrine: the skull holds brain tissue, blood and CSF, and when one increases, ICP rises once the others can no longer make room). Morning headache, headache with coughing or bending, vomiting and papilledema are its hallmark signs.

Seizure: tongue biting and incontinence happen during a tonic-clonic seizure. Drowsiness can be postictal or a sign of increased ICP, so the nurse checks whether it improves over the next hour; if it does not, or worsens, it is reported.

Types of brain tumors: gliomas arise from the brain's supporting (glial) cells; glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults, grows quickly and infiltrates surrounding brain. Meningiomas arise from the meninges, are usually benign and slow-growing, and press on the brain from outside. Metastases from cancers such as lung, breast and melanoma are the most common brain tumors overall (which is why her chest, abdomen and pelvis were scanned). Any of them can cause headache, seizures and focal deficits.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 57-year-old female client brought in by her husband after a seizure at home.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The nurse documents the seizure the husband described as a [[drop0]]. The client's signs of increased ICP are mainly caused by [[drop1]], which is expected to improve with [[drop2]], so the nurse monitors her for [[drop3]].

options.text: focal impaired awareness seizure that progressed to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure

question.explanation:
Seizure type: staring and not answering (impaired awareness) with lip smacking and picking at her clothing (automatisms) is a focal impaired awareness seizure; it then spread to both sides of the brain (stiffening and jerking of the whole body), a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Describing the start of a seizure accurately helps the team classify it. A first seizure in adulthood always prompts a search for a cause such as a tumor.

Vasogenic edema: the tumor's abnormal blood vessels leak fluid through a damaged blood-brain barrier into the surrounding white matter. Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) stabilize the barrier and reduce this swelling. Cytotoxic edema is different: brain cells swell when they lack oxygen (ischemia, a prolonged seizure) and corticosteroids do not help it.

Adverse effects of dexamethasone: high blood glucose (the most common), stomach irritation (given with food, often with a stomach-protecting drug), insomnia, mood changes, infection risk and, over time, thrush and muscle weakness. Glucose is checked as ordered and high readings are reported.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 57-year-old female client brought in by her husband after a seizure at home.

question.stem: The nurse plans care to keep the client safe and prevent increases in ICP before surgery. For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees with her head in line with her body
Encourage her to cough forcefully every hour to keep her lungs clear
Give the stool softener and teach her not to strain or hold her breath during bowel movements
Keep the bed low with the side rails padded and up
Check her capillary glucose as ordered and report high readings
Lay her flat with her legs raised when she has a headache
Watch for drowsiness, dizziness, and mood changes after starting levetiracetam
Apply wrist restraints if she becomes restless

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Provider Orders.
question.explanation:
Indicated: the head of the bed at 30 degrees with the head aligned helps venous blood drain from the brain. Straining and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre) raise pressure in the chest and head, so a stool softener and teaching prevent it. A low bed with padded rails protects her if she has another seizure. Dexamethasone raises blood glucose, so glucose is checked and high values are reported. Levetiracetam commonly causes drowsiness and dizziness (fall risk) and can cause irritability or low mood, which can be mistaken for tumor effects, so the nurse watches and reports.

Contraindicated: forceful coughing raises ICP; deep breathing and gentle coughing are used instead. Lying flat with the legs raised reduces venous drainage from the head and raises ICP. Restraints increase agitation and ICP and can cause injury.

Linking the plan to the Monro-Kellie doctrine: each measure limits an increase in one of the three volumes in the skull: brain tissue (swelling; reduced with dexamethasone), blood (venous drainage, avoiding straining, fever and too much sedation, since high CO₂ widens brain blood vessels) and CSF (watching for headache, vomiting and drowsiness that could mean blocked CSF flow, called non-communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 57-year-old female client brought in by her husband after a seizure at home.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Withhold medication until the seizure has lasted 15 minutes
Apply oxygen and have suction ready
Monitor her breathing and level of sedation after the lorazepam is given
Insert a padded tongue blade between her teeth
Call for help and notify the provider
Turn the client onto her side
Restrain her arms and legs to prevent injury

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 3 1500 and Day 4 0710 and the Provider Orders from Day 3 1500.
question.explanation:
The seizure has lasted more than 5 minutes: this is status epilepticus, a medical emergency. The longer it lasts, the less likely it is to stop on its own, and continuous neuronal firing causes hypoxia, excitotoxic (cytotoxic) brain injury and rising ICP.

Correct: a side-lying position lets saliva drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway. Lorazepam is given as ordered; it can depress breathing and cause deep sedation, so the nurse watches her breathing and level of consciousness afterwards. Oxygen and suction treat the hypoxia (dusky lips). Hypoglycemia can cause or prolong seizures, and dexamethasone affects glucose, so the glucose is checked. Help is needed to manage the airway, drugs and monitoring, and the provider must be notified.

Incorrect: restraints can cause fractures and soft tissue injury; nearby objects are moved and the head is protected instead. Nothing is put in the mouth. Waiting to treat lets the seizure become harder to stop and the brain injury worse.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it shows that an expected outcome has been met or that it requires follow-up.

rows.text: No seizures since Day 4
Capillary glucose 14.8 mmol/L before supper
Headache 2/10 with no vomiting

White patches on the tongue and inner cheeks
“I won't drive until my doctor tells me it's safe.”
Husband's plan for managing a seizure at home

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Diagnostic Results from Day 5, the Nurses' Notes from Day 9 1000 and 1030, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Outcomes met: no further seizures on the increased levetiracetam dose; less headache and no vomiting (edema and ICP reduced after resection and dexamethasone); a healing incision. In Canada, a seizure leads to a period without driving set by provincial rules and the provider, and she understands this. The husband's plan is correct: protect, side-lying, time the seizure, and call 911 at 5 minutes.

Require follow-up: dexamethasone-induced hyperglycemia (glucocorticoids raise hepatic glucose production and insulin resistance) needs to be reported for treatment. White patches that do not wipe off suggest oral candidiasis (thrush) from corticosteroid immunosuppression. Stopping dexamethasone suddenly can cause adrenal insufficiency and rebound cerebral edema: it must be tapered as prescribed, so this statement needs further teaching.

description: 57-year-old female client with a first seizure in adulthood from a glioblastoma: recognizing signs of increased ICP, focal deficits and seizure features, documenting the seizure type, vasogenic edema and dexamethasone adverse effects, a care plan that keeps her safe and prevents rises in ICP, status epilepticus after craniotomy, and corticosteroid effects at discharge.

authorReview.note:
Case written by Claude on 2 Nov 2026 for the Unit 7 learning outcomes and revised the same day to be more nursing-focused; please review before using it with students:
- Revised 2 Nov 2026 to the nursing-focused rules: screen 2 now sorts findings into tumor location, increased ICP and seizure (tumor types in the rationale); screen 3 adds the dexamethasone adverse effect; screen 4 is a nursing care plan (Monro-Kellie and hydrocephalus in the rationale); screen 5 adds monitoring after lorazepam.
- The capillary glucose target (4.0–7.0 mmol/L before meals) is the Diabetes Canada target, not an MCC laboratory range.
- Clinician review: dexamethasone, levetiracetam and lorazepam orders.
